# Introduction

## Why a Quarto website?

-   Typically people build websites in drag-and-drop website builders or by
    writing HTML by hand. Each has a learning curve and often a monthly cost.

-   Content and layout get tangled together, so changing the look of a site
    means editing every page.

-   It can be hard to see what changed, who changed it, or to go back to an
    earlier version.

-   Moving a site between tools or hosting providers is a lot of manual
    labour ..... and error prone

## What is Quarto?

-   An open-source scientific and technical publishing system that allows you
    to create documents, presentations, books and websites from plain text
    files.

-   You write in Markdown, a lightweight markup language for creating
    formatted text using a plain-text editor. It was designed by [John Gruber
    in 2004](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/). Quarto turns it
    into web pages.

-   Quarto can also run code (R, Python, Julia and Observable) and put the
    results in your pages. We do not need that today, but your site can grow
    to include it.

-   This website is a Quarto website.

## What are GitHub and GitHub Pages?

-   [GitHub](https://github.com/) is a website for storing and sharing files
    in a **repository**. It keeps a complete history of every change.

-   [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/) is a free service that turns the
    files in a repository into a website with an address like
    `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/YOUR-REPOSITORY/`

-   GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation. We will use it to run
    Quarto for us, so that nothing needs to be installed on your computer.

## How the pieces fit together

Every time you save a change to your repository, the following happens
automatically:

1.  You edit a file in your web browser and save ("commit") the change.

2.  GitHub Actions starts a small computer in the cloud, installs Quarto and
    turns your `.qmd` files into web pages.

3.  GitHub Pages publishes the web pages at your website address.

It takes a minute or two from saving to seeing the change on your website.

# Exercises

## Scenario

You have been asked to create a small website for yourself, your group or
your project. It should have a home page, an about page, a navbar to move
between them and a look of its own.

By the end of this workshop you will have a live website at an address you can
share.

Throughout, we use the repository name `my-first-quarto-site`. You are welcome
to choose your own name. Wherever you see `YOUR-USERNAME` in the instructions,
replace it with your own GitHub username.

## Part 1: Set up a GitHub account {#part-1}

If you already have a GitHub account, sign in at <https://github.com/login>
and skip to [Part 2](#part-2).

🎬 Open a new browser tab and go to <https://github.com/signup>

You can sign up in one of three ways. Choose the one you decided on in the
[pre-course instructions](before.qmd) and follow the matching steps.

### Option 1: Continue with Google

🎬 Click **Continue with Google**

🎬 Choose your Google account and allow GitHub to use it to sign in

🎬 If GitHub asks you to choose a username, see [Choosing a
username](#choosing-a-username) below

### Option 2: Use your Microsoft email address

GitHub does not currently have a "Continue with Microsoft" button[^1]. You can
still sign up with a Microsoft email address (an Outlook or Hotmail address, or
a Microsoft work or school address) by using the email form.

🎬 Type your Microsoft email address into the **Email** box and click
**Continue**

🎬 Create a password. Use a long one that you do not use anywhere else

🎬 Choose a username, see [Choosing a username](#choosing-a-username) below

🎬 Complete the puzzle if GitHub shows you one

🎬 GitHub emails you a code. Open your Microsoft inbox, find the email from
GitHub and type the code into the box on the sign-up page

[^1]: GitHub's help pages say that, at the time of writing, Google and Apple are the
    sign-in providers GitHub supports when you create an account. Sign-up
    screens do change from time to time, so follow the on-screen prompts if
    they differ from these instructions.

### Option 3: Use any other email address

The steps are exactly the same as Option 2, but with an email address from any
other provider, such as your university, your employer or a personal address.

### Choosing a username

Your username is public and it becomes part of your website address, for
example `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/`. Choose something you are happy to
share with colleagues and collaborators.

-   Letters, numbers and single hyphens work best
-   Short is better
-   You can change your username later but your website address will change
    with it

### Finishing up

🎬 If GitHub asks you to personalise your experience, you can skip it

🎬 If asked to choose a plan, choose the free plan (**Continue for free**)

🎬 Check you can see the GitHub home page with your username or avatar in the
top right corner

::: {.callout-tip title="Verify your email and keep your account safe"}
You need a verified email address to create repositories. If GitHub has asked
you for a code, make sure you have entered it. GitHub also recommends
turning on two-factor authentication (2FA) or a passkey, which you can do after
the course in your account settings.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Sign out and then sign back in using the same route you used to sign up
(Google, or your email and password). The menu for signing out is under your
avatar in the top right corner. Making sure you can get back in now saves a
lot of worry later.
:::

## Part 2: Create a repository and publish it {#part-2}

### Create a repository

A repository (or "repo") is a project folder stored on GitHub. Your website
will live in one.

🎬 Click the **+** in the top right corner of GitHub | **New repository**

🎬 Fill in the form:

-   Repository name: `my-first-quarto-site`[^2]

-   Description: optional

-   Choose **Public**[^3]

-   Tick **Add a README file**

-   Leave everything else as it is

🎬 Click **Create repository**

[^2]: The repository name becomes part of your website address, so keep it
    short, with lower case letters, numbers and hyphens, and no spaces.

[^3]: GitHub Pages is free for public repositories. Anyone on the internet can
    see the files in a public repository and your website will be public too, so do
    not put anything private in it.

You now have a repository containing one file, `README.md`.

### Turn on GitHub Pages

🎬 Click the **Settings** tab at the top of your repository[^4]

🎬 In the left menu, click **Pages**

🎬 Under **Build and deployment**, find **Source** and choose **GitHub
Actions** from the drop-down list

[^4]: On a narrow screen the tabs are hidden behind a **...** button.

This tells GitHub that you will provide instructions (a "workflow") for
building your website. We will add the workflow shortly. The setting saves
itself, so there is nothing else to click.

### Add the Quarto configuration file

Every Quarto website has a configuration file called `_quarto.yml`. It
describes the website. Note the underscore at the start of the name.

🎬 Click the **Code** tab to go back to your files

🎬 Click **Add file** | **Create new file**

🎬 In the name box, type `_quarto.yml`

🎬 Paste this into the big text box:

``` yml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My first Quarto site"
```

🎬 Click **Commit changes...** and then, in the box that appears, leave
**Commit directly to the main branch** selected and click **Commit changes**[^5]

[^5]: "Committing" is Git's word for saving a snapshot of your changes with a
    short message about what you did. GitHub keeps every commit so you can see
    the history of your project and go back to any earlier version.

🚨 Indentation matters in YAML. Make sure `title` is indented two spaces
under `website`, and `type` is indented two spaces under `project`.

### Add the home page

🎬 Click **Add file** | **Create new file**

🎬 In the name box, type `index.qmd`

🎬 Paste this into the big text box:

``` markdown
---
title: "Hello, world!"
---

This is my first Quarto website.
```

🎬 Click **Commit changes...** and then **Commit changes**

`index.qmd` is the file that becomes your home page. The part between the
three dashes is the YAML header which describes the page. The rest is the
content.

### Add the publishing workflow

The last file tells GitHub to build and publish the website every time you
save a change. It has to be in a particular folder.

🎬 Click **Add file** | **Create new file**

🎬 In the name box, type `.github/workflows/publish.yml`. Notice that each
time you type a `/`, GitHub turns what you typed into a folder

🎬 Paste this into the big text box:

``` yml
name: Publish Quarto site to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render the Quarto project
        run: quarto render

      - name: Configure GitHub Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v5

      - name: Upload the site
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

You do not need to understand every line today. In short:

-   `on` says when to run: every time you commit to the `main` branch
-   `build` installs Quarto and turns your `.qmd` files into a website (`quarto render`)
-   `deploy` publishes that website with GitHub Pages

🎬 Click **Commit changes...** and then **Commit changes**

🚨 The most common problem is indentation. If your workflow fails, compare it
carefully with the one above.

### Watch your website being built

🎬 Click the **Actions** tab

You will see a workflow run called "Publish Quarto site to GitHub Pages". A
yellow circle means it is running, a green tick means it worked and a red
cross means something went wrong.

🎬 Wait for the green tick. This usually takes a minute or two

🎬 Click **Settings** | **Pages**. At the top you will see the address of your
website. It looks like `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/my-first-quarto-site/`

🎬 Click **Visit site**, and bookmark your website

::: {.callout-tip title="Troubleshooting"}
If the workflow shows a red cross, click it, then click the failed step to
read the error. Check that:

-   In **Settings** | **Pages**, the Source is **GitHub Actions**
-   The files are called exactly `_quarto.yml` and `index.qmd`, including
    the underscore and the lower case letters
-   The workflow is at exactly `.github/workflows/publish.yml`
-   The indentation matches the examples

You can re-run a failed workflow by clicking **Re-run all jobs**.

If the workflow has a green tick but the website says "404", wait a minute
and refresh the page.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Share the address of your website with the person next to you or in the chat.
Can you find out what the address of their website is?
:::

## Part 3: Create website content with Quarto {#part-3}

### Edit a page

🎬 In the **Code** tab, click `index.qmd`

🎬 Click the pencil icon (**Edit this file**) at the top right of the file

🎬 Change the sentence below the header to something about you, your group
or your project

🎬 Click **Commit changes...** and then **Commit changes**

🎬 Click the **Actions** tab, wait for the green tick and then refresh your
website

This is the rhythm of working with a Quarto website on GitHub: **edit, commit,
wait, refresh**. It is slower than previewing on your own computer, so make a
few changes before each commit.

::: {.callout-tip title="Keep two windows open"}
Keep your website in one tab and your repository in another. After each commit,
swap to the website tab and refresh it once the **Actions** tab shows a green
tick.
:::

### Edit the YAML header

The YAML header sits between the two lines of three dashes at the top of every
`.qmd` file. It holds information about the page such as its title.

🎬 Edit `index.qmd` and change the YAML header to:

``` yml
---
title: "Hello, I'm Your Name"
subtitle: "Welcome to my first Quarto website"
author: "Your Name"
date: last-modified
---
```

🎬 Replace "Your Name" with your own name

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

🚨 YAML is fussy. Keep the quote marks, keep the colon followed by a space
and do not remove the dashes. If your website stops building, look at the
header first.

### Headings and text

Quarto pages are written in Markdown. Here are the most useful bits of syntax.

| Markdown Syntax | Output |
|:-------------------------|:-------------------------|
| `# Header 1` | A first level heading (the biggest) |
| `## Header 2` | A second level heading |
| `### Header 3` | A third level heading |
| `*italics*` | *italics* |
| `**bold**` | **bold** |
| `***bold italics***` | ***bold italics*** |
| `~~strikethrough~~` | ~~strikethrough~~ |
| `` `verbatim code` `` | `verbatim code` |

For lists, start each line with a dash for a bulleted list or with `1.`, `2.`
and so on for a numbered list. Leave a blank line before the list.

🎬 Delete the sentence in `index.qmd` and replace it with the text below, making
the content your own:

::: blockquote
This is **my** website, built with Quarto and GitHub Pages. You will find:

-   Information about me
-   Links to my work
-   Things I am interested in
:::

🎬 Make one word *italic*

🎬 Add a second level heading called `## What I do` and a short paragraph below it

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

### Links and images

| Markdown Syntax | Output |
|:-------------------------|:-------------------------|
| `[Quarto](https://quarto.org)` | [Quarto](https://quarto.org) |
| `![Caption](photo.jpg)` | An image with a caption |
| `![Caption](photo.jpg){width="300"}` | An image 300 pixels wide |

The text in square brackets before an image is its caption and its
description for people using screen readers. Please always write one.

🎬 Add a sentence to `index.qmd` with a link to a website you like

🎬 Add a picture to your repository. Choose a small picture on your
computer (a JPG or PNG under about 1 MB works best). In your repository, click
**Add file** | **Upload files**, drag the picture in, then click **Commit
changes**

🎬 Edit `index.qmd` and add the picture, using the exact name of your file:

``` markdown
![A short description of the picture](photo.jpg){width="300"}
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

🚨 File names on GitHub Pages are case sensitive. `Photo.JPG` and `photo.jpg` are
different files, and the website will show a broken picture if the name in
`index.qmd` does not match the file exactly.

### Add a second page

🎬 Click **Add file** | **Create new file** and call it `about.qmd`

🎬 Add this text and make it about you:

``` markdown
---
title: "About"
---

I work on ...

## Contact

You can find me at ...
```

🎬 Commit the changes

🎬 Edit `index.qmd` and add a link to your new page:

``` markdown
Read more [about me](about.qmd).
```

Notice that you link to the `.qmd` file. Quarto changes the link to the web
page when it builds the website.

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

### Callouts

Callouts draw attention to some text. They are made with a "div", which is a
group of lines between a line starting with three colons and a line with only
three colons.

🎬 Add a callout to `index.qmd`:

``` markdown
::: {.callout-tip title="Did you know?"}
Quarto turns plain text into web pages.
:::
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

There are five types of callout: `note`, `tip`, `important`, `warning` and
`caution`. Change `callout-tip` to `callout-note` and see what happens.

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Can you add a callout with the type `warning` and the title "Work in
progress" to the bottom of your home page?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Can you add a third page called `projects.qmd`, with a title, a bulleted
list of three projects and a link from `about.qmd` to the new page?
:::

## Part 4: Create a navbar {#part-4}

So far, the only way to get from one page to another is by following links
that you typed. A navbar is a menu bar across the top of every page. It is
described in `_quarto.yml`.

### Add a navbar

🎬 Click `_quarto.yml` and then the pencil icon (**Edit this file**)

🎬 Replace the contents with:

``` yml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My first Quarto site"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Home"
        href: index.qmd
      - text: "About"
        href: about.qmd
```

🎬 Commit the changes, wait for the green tick and refresh your website

You should see a bar across the top of your website with the title of your
site and two links. Let us look at how the file is organised:

-   `navbar` is inside `website`, so it is indented two spaces
-   `left` is inside `navbar`, so it is indented four spaces. It is the list of
    links on the left of the bar
-   Each link starts with a dash `-` and has a `text` (what visitors see)
    and an `href` (the page it goes to)

🚨 Use spaces, never tabs, and keep the indentation exactly as shown.

### Add more to the navbar

🎬 Edit `_quarto.yml` and add a search box and a link to your repository on the
right side of the bar. Replace `YOUR-USERNAME` with your username:

``` yml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My first Quarto site"
  navbar:
    search: true
    left:
      - text: "Home"
        href: index.qmd
      - text: "About"
        href: about.qmd
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/my-first-quarto-site
        aria-label: GitHub repository
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Add your `projects.qmd` page to the navbar. If you did not make it, make it
now.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Navbar links can also be grouped into a drop-down menu using `menu`. Can you
find out how by looking at the [Quarto navigation
guide](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-navigation.html) and make a
drop-down menu called "More" that holds your About and Projects pages?
:::

## Part 5: Change the look of your site with `styles.css` {#part-5}

Quarto websites are made of HTML, which says *what* is on the page, and CSS
(Cascading Style Sheets), which says *how it looks*. Quarto writes the HTML for
you, and you can add your own CSS in a file called `styles.css` to change the
colours, fonts and layout.

### Create the stylesheet

🎬 Click **Add file** | **Create new file** and call it `styles.css`

🎬 Paste this into the big text box:

``` css
/* css styles */

h1, h2, h3 {
  color: #58579B; /* blue */
}
```

🎬 Click **Commit changes...** and then **Commit changes**

Nothing will change on your website yet, because Quarto does not know about
your stylesheet.

### Tell Quarto to use your stylesheet

🎬 Edit `_quarto.yml` and add this to the end, at the very left edge (it is
not inside `website`):

``` yml
format:
  html:
    css: styles.css
```

🎬 Commit the changes, wait for the green tick and refresh your website. Your
headings should now be blue

A CSS rule has three parts:

-   A **selector** says what to change. Here `h1, h2, h3` means "the first,
    second and third level headings"
-   A **property** says what aspect to change. Here `color` is the text colour
-   A **value** says what to change it to. Here `#58579B` is a colour written as
    a hexadecimal code. You can also use colour names such as `tomato` or
    `teal`

🎬 Change the colour to one you like. Search the web for "colour picker" to
find codes for other colours

### Style the navbar

🎬 Edit `styles.css` and add these rules to the end:

``` css
/* Style the navbar */
.navbar {
  background-color: #2E2D62 !important; /* navy */
}

.navbar .navbar-brand,
.navbar .navbar-title,
.navbar .nav-link {
  color: #FFFFFF !important; /* white */
}

.navbar .nav-link:hover {
  color: #FA6862 !important; /* pink */
}
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

The `!important` tells the browser that your rule wins over Quarto's own
styling. It is a heavy hammer, so use it only when a change does not seem to
work.

::: {.callout-tip title="Find out what to change"}
Not sure what to call the thing you want to change? In your browser, right-click
the part of your website and choose **Inspect**. The panel that opens shows the
HTML for that spot, including the name of its class (the bit that starts with a
dot in your CSS).
:::

### Change the font

🎬 Edit `styles.css` and add this to the very top of the file, above everything
else:

``` css
@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=DM+Sans:wght@400;700&display=swap');

body {
  font-family: 'DM Sans', sans-serif;
}
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

🚨 An `@import` line must come before all of the other rules. If your font does
not change, check it is at the top of the file.

### Make your own box

You can also make your own styles and then use them on any part of a page.
Earlier you made a callout, which is a div with a style. You can make your own.

🎬 Add this to the end of `styles.css`:

``` css
/* My own style: a highlighted box */
.highlight-box {
  background-color: #E0F1FA; /* light blue */
  border-left: 6px solid #29A69D; /* teal */
  padding: 1rem;
  margin: 1rem 0;
}
```

🎬 Edit `index.qmd` and add this to the page:

``` markdown
::: {.highlight-box}
This text is in a box styled by **my** CSS.
:::
```

🎬 Commit the changes and refresh your website

::: {.callout-important title="Challenge"}
Choose a palette of three colours for your website and use it for the
headings, the navbar and the highlighted box. Can you also change the
colours of the `callout-tip` callout you made earlier? Use the Inspect trick to
find the names you need.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Prefer a ready-made look?"}
Quarto comes with a collection of ready-made themes. Add a line to `_quarto.yml`
and your own `styles.css` still works on top of it:

``` yml
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    css: styles.css
```

You can see the others in the [Quarto themes
guide](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html).
:::

# Summary

-   Quarto is a publishing system that turns plain text files into websites,
    documents and more.

-   GitHub stores your files with a full history of changes, and GitHub Pages
    publishes your website for free from a repository.

-   You can sign up to GitHub with a Google account, a Microsoft email
    address or any other email address.

-   A GitHub Actions workflow in `.github/workflows` runs Quarto for you each
    time you commit, so you do not need to install anything.

-   `_quarto.yml` describes the whole website and `.qmd` files are the pages.
    The YAML header at the top of each page gives its title and other details.

-   Markdown is used to make headings, lists, links and images. "Divs" group
    content together to make callouts or to apply your own styling.

-   The navbar is built in `_quarto.yml` with a list of links.

-   `styles.css` changes the look of the website with rules made of a
    selector, a property and a value.

# Where next?

-   Quarto's [website guide](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) shows how to
    add blogs, listings and more

-   The [Markdown basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html)
    page has more syntax like tables and equations

-   [GitHub Pages documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/pages) explains how
    to use your own domain name

-   Set up two-factor authentication or a passkey for your GitHub account

-   Quarto can also run R or Python code and put the results in your pages. The
    [Reproducible reports with
    Quarto](https://ukri-digital-research-skills-catalyst.github.io/quarto-intro/)
    workshop shows you how

Good luck on your future Quarto projects!
